LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

Face pattern — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This card sits between the faces and the pure patterns in your set: features built from bold shapes. This lesson uses it to stretch your baby’s looking a few seconds longer.

What is this?

A face pattern is a face whose features are made of decorative shapes rather than plain circles and curves — half portrait, half design. For a baby it doubles the interest: the face pulls the gaze in, the patterns hold it there.

What does it mean?

Young attention is a muscle before it is a habit. Detailed images give it something to do: the eye travels from shape to shape, resting and restarting. Faces with built-in detail reliably stretch fixation past what a plain shape manages.

What does the child need to know?

Your finger is the tour guide here. Tracing slowly, one shape per visit, turns a still card into a moving one — and a moving target is what young eyes follow longest. Do not name every shape; "so many patterns!" carries the whole lesson.

Why this matters

Sustained attention at three months predicts nothing and promises nothing — but it practises something: the feeling of staying with one thing. That feeling is the raw material of every later puzzle, book and conversation.

What it teaches

Visual attention span, smooth eye travel across an image, shape interest, and calm shared focus — parent and baby attending to the same thing at the same time, which is joint attention in its earliest form.

Words to learn

patternsshapeslooktracelinesface

Say this to your child

“"Look at this face — it is made of patterns! Lines here, shapes there. My finger is going for a little walk... round and round, up and down. Look at all these patterns on one face."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at close range in good light and give it its name: "A pattern face. So many shapes."
  2. Let your baby find it alone first — ten seconds of free looking before you do anything at all.
  3. Then trace one pattern with your fingertip, slowly, from one end to the other, saying nothing or nearly nothing.
  4. Rest your finger, count three breaths, and trace a different shape — one tour at a time, no grand tours.
  5. Hand the session back to your baby: card still, voice quiet, and watch where the eyes wander next. That wandering is the workout.

Look closer at the picture

What the artwork verifiably shows: a face whose features are built from bold high-contrast shapes inside the outline. Name the shapes you actually see rather than inventing detail, and keep the richer question for the live picture — where do your baby’s eyes land first?

Ask your child

Watch the travel: do the eyes hop between shapes or slide? Does your tracing finger collect the gaze and lead it? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which shape is the favourite — I will start there tomorrow."

What your child can say or do

Fixation that outlasts the plainer cards, eyes that shadow your fingertip the whole way, a stillness that looks like study, or a sudden tired glance away — the last one is the honest finish line, not a failure.

Out in the real world

Patterns ride through the whole house: stripes on a shirt, tiles on the kitchen floor, the grill of the radiator. Wherever bold pattern meets your baby’s day, one slow trace with your finger re-runs this lesson in five seconds.

Try it together

Shape walk: lay two or three cards in a gentle arc at focusing distance and let your baby’s gaze travel the arc while you narrate the stops — "here... and here... and here." You are building the habit of looking around, not quizzing.

Understanding check

Ask yourself two things: did the looking last longer today than on a plainer card, and did you manage to stay quiet through at least one full trace? Both grow with practice — yours and the baby’s.

Parent tips

If your baby loses the card mid-trace, start the trace again from the top without comment; restarting is normal at this age. Keep your voice lower than you think it needs to be — quiet is what makes detail visible to a new brain.

Staying safe

Trace with a clean, dry hand — this card will spend its life near a newborn, and feeds happen fast. Lying-down sessions belong on a firm surface with you alongside; never leave a young baby propped with a card in reach.

This lesson pairs with the Face pattern flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).
